blocks.text: This helps frame an interpretive question raised by the passage: Paul's rhetorical questions claim rights to food and drink, travel with a believing wife, and refrain from manual work, naming Barnabas in the comparison. Establishes compensation and household-support claims before Paul's contextual nonuse is considered. Paul refuses to activate the rights just defended and describes offering the gospel without charge as his chosen ground of boasting, while proclamation itself is an entrusted necessity. Prevents both sale of spiritual access and compulsory imitation of Paul's exceptional financial strategy. Paul says he and coworkers did not use the right but endured anything so as not to place an obstacle before the Messiah's gospel. This helps frame an interpretive question raised by the passage: Keeps voluntary nonuse distinct from compulsory unpaid labor or an institutional rule that faithful workers must refuse wages. Paul argues from sowing spiritual things to reaping material things and notes that others already share a right over the Corinthians. Recognizes legitimate support without turning spiritual benefit into an unpriced debt controlled by the teacher. Paul appeals to temple workers sharing sacrificial food and says the Lord directed gospel announcers to live from the gospel. Strengthens the maintenance right while requiring separate interpretation of the Jesus tradition and its modern institutional form. This helps frame an interpretive question raised by the passage: Paul compares runners and boxers with his own purposeful discipline so that he will not be disqualified after proclaiming to others. This helps frame an interpretive question raised by the passage: Paul's right to material support and voluntary renunciation cannot justify prosperity extraction, unpaid coercive labor, or denying workers fair compensation. Becoming all things to all people describes mission adaptation under gospel constraint; it cannot authorize deception, colonial domination, or erasure of vulnerable cultures. Athletic discipline is metaphorical and must not support eating disorders, self-harm, abusive training, or contempt for disabled bodies.
